entries.clue: Condiment that’s hot in cold starter from Indian (6)

indicatorNotes.starter from: the starter of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a noun for a cold, the kind you catch

annotation.surface: A diner notes that a fiery sauce comes in a cold appetiser at an Indian restaurant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot in cold' looks like an instruction to put H inside a word for cold; it is not — 'that's hot' belongs to the definition and 'in' only links.
annotation.definitionFit: Chilli is a hot spice used to flavour food, so it is a condiment that's hot.

entries.clue: Member one criticises makes laws (10)

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, or member, of the body
to slate is to criticise harshly

annotation.surface: A parliamentary member complains that one colleague criticises how laws get made.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Member' pretends to be a Member of Parliament, fitting the law-making scene, but it is a body part. To slate is British for to criticise severely.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb comes from legislation, the making of laws, and both sides are third-person present.

entries.clue: Problem for driver in boring old Phoenician city (4,4)

blocks.note: Tyre was a Phoenician port, now in Lebanon

annotation.surface: A motorist has trouble while stuck in a dull ancient city on the Mediterranean coast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Driver' could be a golf club or a slave driver; here it is a motorist, and TYRE is the British spelling of tire.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a puncture is one of the commonest roadside troubles a motorist meets.

entries.clue: American friend had to convert founder of a religion (6)

indicatorNotes.to convert: converting the letters of HAD changes them into a new order

blocks.note: bud, short for buddy, is American for friend

annotation.surface: An American's friend was obliged to convert to follow the founder of a faith.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had to convert' reads as a religious conversion, which suits the founder of a religion; in fact only the three letters of 'had' are converted.
annotation.definitionFit: The Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, founded Buddhism.

entries.clue: Bishop always conceals untruth for person with faith (8)

indicatorNotes.conceals: EVER conceals LIE by holding it inside

annotation.surface: A bishop who habitually hides a falsehood — hardly fitting for a man of faith.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lying cleric, the opposite of the believer he should be.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who believes is one who holds a faith, usually a religious one.

entries.clue: Perverts or some antibourgeois Trots idling around (8)

indicatorNotes.some: some of the words: the answer is part of the string
indicatorNotes.around: turned around, the hidden string reads backwards

blocks.note: the letters spanning antibourgeoiS TROTS IDling

annotation.surface: A jibe at Trotskyists, lazy revolutionaries lounging about while railing against the middle class.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perverts' is a verb here (twists, misrepresents), not a noun for people. Trots is slang for Trotskyists.
annotation.definitionFit: To pervert something, such as the truth, is to distort it.

entries.clue: How steak may be cooked that’s good for you! (4,4)

blocks.note: the doneness grade for steak cooked right through, past medium
an exclamation of praise, congratulating someone

annotation.surface: A cook claims a thoroughly cooked steak is the healthy choice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That's good for you' reads as a health claim about the steak; it is really the exclamation of congratulation.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrase: the kitchen term for steak cooked through, and the idiom of praise, 'Well done!', said just as 'Good for you!' is.

entries.clue: Exclude from old American university (4)

annotation.surface: Someone is barred from an old American college.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Exclude from' as one phrase about expulsion; 'from' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to leave something out is to exclude it.

entries.clue: Snake-like fish in small shelter, turning around (4)

indicatorNotes.turning around: turning the pieces around reads them backwards

blocks.note: S = small, as in clothing sizes
the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind

annotation.surface: Fish that look like snakes wriggle around in a little hiding place.
annotation.walkthrough: The lee is a sailing word for the side sheltered from the wind, hence shelter.
annotation.definitionFit: Eels are long, slender fish that look like snakes.

entries.clue: Ultimately endure conclusions of Royal Family (6)

indicatorNotes.conclusions of: the conclusion of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: last letters of RoyaL and FamilY

annotation.surface: Advice that, in the end, one must put up with the ways of the royals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately endure' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the single first word and 'endure' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Ultimately and lastly both mean in the end.

entries.clue: Faulty hearing – Mr Ali’s troubled with it (8)

indicatorNotes.troubled: troubled letters are stirred up into a new order

annotation.surface: A deaf ear: Mr Ali is bothered by his poor hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Faulty hearing' suggests bad ears; the hearing is a court case.
annotation.definitionFit: A mistrial is a trial, or court hearing, invalidated by an error.

entries.clue: Liam and Noel playing with toy in a way that arouses feelings (11)

annotation.definition: in a way that arouses feelings

indicatorNotes.playing with: playing with letters moves them about into a new order

annotation.surface: The Gallagher brothers of Oasis perform with feeling, or play with a toy.
annotation.walkthrough: Liam and Noel Gallagher are the famously feuding brothers of the British band Oasis, so 'playing' first suggests music.
annotation.definitionFit: Emotionally means in a way that stirs the emotions, or arouses feelings.

entries.clue: Contents of fine thermos that’s nearest the bottom (10)

indicatorNotes.Contents of: the answer is contained within the words that follow

annotation.surface: The drink in a good vacuum flask has settled at the very bottom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contents of' pretends to mean the drink in the flask; it is telling you the answer sits inside the next words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym built from nether, meaning lower, plus the superlative -most: lowest of all.

entries.clue: Ms Blanchett admitting bitterness about having no partner (8)

indicatorNotes.admitting: CATE admits, lets in, the other piece

annotation.surface: The actress confesses resentment about being single.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' in the surface, but it turns BILE around.
annotation.definitionFit: Celibate means abstaining from sex, so having no partner.

entries.clue: Beaten cricketer with England gutted (8)

indicatorNotes.gutted: a gutted word has lost its insides, leaving its outer letters

annotation.surface: A cricketer is beaten, and England are left devastated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, which fits a cricket defeat; here it empties a word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are past participles for struck again and again, or heavily defeated.

entries.clue: In text that’s rewritten, entertaining chapter vanished (7)

indicatorNotes.rewritten: rewritten letters are put down in a new order
indicatorNotes.entertaining: to entertain a guest is to take them in, so the anagram holds C

annotation.surface: A chapter that entertained readers has been cut from the revised edition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a link word: it is part of the anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a species that has died out has vanished from the earth.

entries.clue: Denial, for example, when entering country (8)

annotation.surface: Refusing entry to a country is one example of denial.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For example' reads as part of the sentence about denial; it is the source of EG.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name the act of saying something is not so.

entries.clue: Perhaps May in that place by South Africa’s capital (7)

indicatorNotes.capital: a word's capital is its first letter

annotation.surface: A spring month, perhaps, spent by the South African capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'May' is a person, not a month: Theresa May was British prime minister from 2016 to 2019. 'Perhaps' warns she is only one Theresa.
annotation.definitionFit: Theresa May is an example of someone named Theresa.

entries.clue: Stage make-up isn’t put on musical lead in Phantom (6,5)

indicatorNotes.put on: AINT is put on after the other pieces
indicatorNotes.lead in: the lead in a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A theatre note: no make-up is applied to the leading man in The Phantom of the Opera.
annotation.walkthrough: Phantom and 'lead' suggest the star of that musical, but the musical in the wordplay is Grease.
annotation.definitionFit: Greasepaint is the thick make-up used by stage actors.

entries.clue: Someone who cuts dried fruit, right? (6)

blocks.note: a prune is a dried plum

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether the person who slices dried fruit has it right.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is also a pun: a pruner cuts plants, and a prune is dried fruit.
annotation.definitionFit: An agent noun: the one who prunes, trimming branches from trees and shrubs.

entries.clue: Precious stone in ring put on friend (4)

indicatorNotes.put on: in a down clue, O is put on top of PAL

annotation.surface: A gem set in a ring is placed on a friend's finger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In ring' suggests a gem set in a ring; 'in' only links, and the ring is O.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the iridescent silica gem is one of many precious stones.

entries.clue: Don’t eat the kind of food served at McDonald’s (4)

annotation.definition2: the kind of food served at McDonald’s

blocks.note: an imperative verb: go without food

blocks.clueFragment: the kind of food served at McDonald’s
blocks.note: the quick-service category burger chains belong to

annotation.surface: Advice to avoid burger-chain food.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one piece of dietary advice, but it splits after 'eat': a command, then a description of a type of food.
annotation.definitionFit: Fasting means not eating, and McDonald's serves fast food.

entries.clue: MP has not drunk spirits (8)

indicatorNotes.drunk: drunk letters stagger into a new order

annotation.surface: A sober Member of Parliament has not drunk any liquor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' as liquor fits the drinking surface; here they are ghosts.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the ghostly sense of spirits, not the bottled one.

entries.clue: Laud unclothed couple’s childminder (2,4)

indicatorNotes.unclothed: with its clothes, its outer letters, taken off, only the middle is left

blocks.note: a couple is a pair; 's = has, joining the pieces

annotation.surface: Someone praises a naked couple's nanny.
annotation.walkthrough: An au pair is a young foreign helper who lives with a family and looks after the children.
annotation.definitionFit: An au pair is employed to mind children.

entries.clue: Leo stole crackers, getting release from captivity (3,5)

indicatorNotes.crackers: crackers means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: Leo pinched some biscuits and was freed from prison.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' looks like the biscuits Leo stole; it is British slang for crazy, telling you to scramble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To let loose is to set free, releasing from captivity.

entries.clue: Saw blade’s edges grasped (6)

indicatorNotes.edges: a word's edges are its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A saw's cutting edges have been gripped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' pretends to be the cutting tool alongside 'blade'; it is the past tense of see.
annotation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, so it means saw.
